newsitem.title: FRANCE: French teachers call strike, add to labour unrest.
newsitem.headline: French teachers call strike, add to labour unrest.

text.p: On the day France's 12.5 million pupils began a new school year, five trade unions representing some 825,000 teachers called a one-day strike for September 30 to protest against planned job and budget cuts.

The call issued by all the main teaching unions was the first shot in what union leaders have warned could be a "hot autumn" of labour unrest over government austerity plans, mounting layoffs, record unemployment and wages.
A joint statement by the five unions said the strike was in protest at a draft 1997 education budget they said was "in decline for the first time in decades" featuring 2,300 job cuts.

Polls show French voters widely expect a new flare-up of labour unrest, possibly matching a 21-day bout of public transport strikes late last year, that could challenge European Union plans for monetary union from 1999.
But two senior union leaders disagreed on Tuesday over the likelihood of major disruption over budget cuts intended to help France qualify for the planned European Union single currency.
"I really don't see it happening," said Nicole Notat, head of the pro-Socialist CFDT, France's largest union federation. But she predicted sporadic strikes in the autumn.
Louis Viannet, general secretary of the Communist-led CGT union, which spearheaded last year's strikes alongside the non-partisan Force Ouvriere, called the economic climate "a catastrophe".

"There is every reason for expressing discontent and for increasing demands," he said. Those expecting a wave of unrest "are not wrong but that doesn't mean to say that it will happen automatically. There are no rules," he said.
Viannet said voters were increasingly fed up since conservative President Jacques Chirac was asking them to continue accepting the same harsh economic policies.
"We're facing a president and a government who are telling us: Things are going badly...we must continue the same policies with the same government," he said.
But while Viannet said the government should abandon the drive for a single European currency, Notat reiterated support for that goal, saying it would help create jobs.

France faces severe budget restrictions to qualify for the currency, but she said: "We must stop saying that it's difficult...People talk about the deficit reduction to forget that the single currency will bring positive things." REUTER
